answer.rationale: With the line at 94% of committed volume and no buffer, delivery risk is the binding constraint alongside the cost mandate. memory_c2 shows the low-cost vendor cut unit cost and onboarded quickly, but that record is silent on performance under tight capacity/no-buffer conditions, so switching now carries unverified delivery risk at the worst possible time. memory_c4 shows that benchmarking against market rates at renewal recovered real margin and improved payment terms with the incumbent, without any migration disruption, consistent with the stability seen in memory_c1 and the volume-pricing gains in memory_c6. Given only one sourcing decision is available this cycle and the contract expires in 14 days, negotiating harder with the incumbent using competitive benchmarks (including the low-cost quote as leverage) is the action most likely to lower TCO while holding delivery risk flat. I verified memory_c2 and memory_c4 because they are the two claims doing the most work in the tradeoff between cost savings and delivery risk. I'm flagging downstream risk because if negotiation doesn't close enough of the 18% gap, a vendor switch or second-sourcing may still be needed next cycle, and that decision should be revisited with fresh, situation-specific evidence rather than assumed from this outcome.
